progressionInfo.name: I-♭III-♭VII-IV Progression
progressionInfo.subtitle: A powerful, anthem-like progression that borrows the ♭III and ♭VII from the parallel minor and Mixolydian mode. By avoiding the standard major key leading tone entirely, it creates the distinctly 'rock' harmonic language heard in classic rock, grunge, and Britpop.

properties.label: I (Tonic)
properties.value: Home chord that anchors the tonal center and provides the foundation for modal borrowing

properties.label: ♭III (Chromatic Mediant)
properties.value: Borrowed from the parallel minor/Aeolian mode, adds a darker, heavier color against the major tonic

properties.label: ♭VII (Subtonic)
properties.value: Borrowed from the Mixolydian mode, avoids leading tone resolution and reinforces the rock sound

properties.label: IV (Subdominant)
properties.value: The only diatonic non-tonic chord, provides a plagal pull back toward the tonic

properties.label: Modal Character
properties.value: Combines Aeolian (♭III) and Mixolydian (♭VII) borrowing to create a uniquely rock harmonic palette

examples.label: ♭III
examples.value: G (G5 power chord: G-D) — borrowed from E minor

examples.label: ♭VII
examples.value: D (D5 power chord: D-A) — borrowed from E Mixolydian

examples.label: Modal Source
examples.value: G is the ♭III from E Aeolian; D is the ♭VII from E Mixolydian (E-F#-G#-A-B-C#-D)

chordDiagrams.title: I-♭III-♭VII-IV in E (Power Chords)
chordDiagrams.description: Power chord voicings for a driving rock sound:
practiceNotes: The G5 is the ♭III, borrowed from E natural minor (Aeolian mode)
The D5 is the ♭VII, borrowed from E Mixolydian mode
Power chords work perfectly here because they omit the 3rd, keeping the modal quality ambiguous
Try palm muting on the lower strings and releasing for dynamic contrast

chordDiagrams.title: I-♭III-♭VII-IV in G Major
chordDiagrams.description: Open and barre chord voicings with borrowed chords:
practiceNotes: B♭ is the ♭III, borrowed from G natural minor (G-A-B♭-C-D-E♭-F)
F is the ♭VII, borrowed from G Mixolydian (G-A-B-C-D-E-F)
The B♭ barre chord requires smooth transitioning from the open G chord
Practice the G to B♭ change slowly — the root moves down by only a whole step

advancedApplications.title: Voicing & Texture Variations
advancedApplications.description: Expand the progression with different guitar textures:
items: Play the ♭III as a full barre chord and the ♭VII as an open chord for tonal contrast
Use arpeggiated picking on the I and IV, switching to strummed chords on the ♭III and ♭VII
Add suspended notes (sus2 or sus4) on the tonic chord to create melodic movement
Layer clean arpeggios over a distorted power chord rhythm for a wall-of-sound effect
Try drop-D tuning and use the open 6th string as a drone under the entire progression

advancedApplications.title: Rhythmic Approaches
advancedApplications.description: Different rhythmic feels to apply to this progression:
items: Straight eighth-note chug with palm muting for a driving punk or grunge feel
Syncopated 16th-note funk strumming to bring out the chord color changes
Half-time feel with sustained power chords for an anthemic, arena-rock sound
Alternating between strummed chords and single-note riffs based on each chord root
Use a triplet shuffle to evoke a bluesy classic rock groove

advancedApplications.title: Key Transposition Guide
items: A Major: A - C - G - D (all open-friendly chords)
C Major: C - E♭ - B♭ - F (requires barre chords on ♭III and ♭VII)
D Major: D - F - C - G (F barre chord is the challenge)
E Major: E - G - D - A (very guitar-friendly with open shapes)
G Major: G - B♭ - F - C (B♭ barre chord adds complexity)

examples.title: "Hey Jude" (Na-Na-Na Section) - The Beatles
examples.description: The iconic coda vamps on a I-♭VII-IV pattern that extends into ♭III territory
examples.detail: One of the most recognizable uses of modal borrowing in pop-rock history

examples.title: "Don't Look Back in Anger" - Oasis
examples.description: Britpop anthem that uses ♭III and ♭VII chords to create sweeping, emotional moments
examples.detail: Noel Gallagher channeled Beatles-style modal interchange into 1990s rock

examples.title: "Whole Lotta Love" - Led Zeppelin
examples.description: Heavy modal rock riff that operates in the space between major and minor
examples.detail: Zeppelin masterfully blurred Aeolian and Mixolydian modes throughout their catalog

examples.title: "Smells Like Teen Spirit" - Nirvana
examples.description: Grunge anthem built on power chords with heavy modal borrowing from the parallel minor
examples.detail: Kurt Cobain embraced the ♭III and ♭VII sound as a punk-influenced rock vocabulary

examples.title: "Sweet Home Alabama" - Lynyrd Skynyrd
examples.description: Southern rock classic using the ♭VII (and related modal patterns) in D major
examples.detail: The modal borrowing gives it the signature floating, non-resolving feel

examples.title: "Champagne Supernova" - Oasis
examples.description: Extended Britpop epic that uses borrowed chords to build emotional intensity
examples.detail: Layers of ♭VII and ♭III movement create the track's anthemic, soaring quality

practiceCategories.title: Chord Transitions
items: Practice the E5-G5-D5-A5 power chord cycle slowly at 60 BPM
Focus on minimizing hand movement between the G5 and D5 shapes
Work on the G major to B♭ barre chord transition in the open-chord version
Use a click track and aim for seamless changes at 100 BPM before speeding up
Practice landing each chord cleanly on beat 1 with no buzzing or muted strings

practiceCategories.title: Rhythm & Dynamics
items: Practice with a driving eighth-note down-strum pattern, accenting beats 2 and 4
Experiment with palm-muting the I and IV chords while letting the ♭III and ♭VII ring open
Try a half-time feel where each chord lasts two full bars for an anthemic sound
Record a rhythm loop and practice switching between clean and overdriven tones
Work on crescendo builds across the four chords, peaking on the IV chord

practiceCategories.title: Modal Soloing
items: Solo using E minor pentatonic over the E power chord version for a bluesy rock sound
Add the major 3rd (G#) over the I chord and flatten it (G) over the ♭III for color
Practice E Mixolydian (E-F#-G#-A-B-C#-D) to outline the ♭VII chord naturally
Target chord tones on each change: E over E5, G/B over G5, D/A over D5, A/E over A5
Combine pentatonic bends with Mixolydian passing tones for an authentic rock lead sound

notatedExercises.title: Exercise 1: Power Chord Vamp in E
notatedExercises.description: Play the I-♭III-♭VII-IV progression using power chords with whole notes to internalize the sound:
practiceNotes: Hold each power chord for a full bar (4 beats)
Listen to the bass note movement: E - G - D - A
Notice how the ♭III (G5) creates a darker shift away from the major tonic
The ♭VII (D5) to IV (A5) movement sets up a satisfying plagal return to I

notatedExercises.title: Exercise 2: Open Chord Strumming in G
notatedExercises.description: Strum the progression using open and barre chords in G major with a steady rock rhythm:
practiceNotes: Use a down-down-up-up-down-up strum pattern per bar
The B♭ barre chord is the biggest challenge — practice the transition from G separately
Start at 80 BPM and increase speed only when changes are clean
Accent the downbeat of each new chord to give the progression forward momentum

notatedExercises.title: Exercise 3: Anthem Rock Pattern with Dynamics
notatedExercises.description: Combine palm muting, open strums, and dynamic swells across the four chords:
practiceNotes: Palm-mute eighth notes on the I chord (E5), then release into an open strum on the ♭III (G5)
Let the ♭VII (D5) ring with sustained strums, building into the IV (A5)
Crescendo from the start of the progression to the IV chord for an anthemic lift
Loop the pattern and focus on making the dynamic shape consistent each cycle

sections.title: Aeolian Mode (♭III Source)
items: E Aeolian (natural minor): E - F# - G - A - B - C - D - E
The ♭III chord (G major) is diatonic to E Aeolian, containing G - B - D
Borrowing ♭III imports the minor 3rd scale degree (G natural instead of G#)
This creates the dark, heavy shift that defines the rock sound of this progression
The ♭III is one of the most common borrowed chords in rock and metal

sections.title: Mixolydian Mode (♭VII Source)
items: E Mixolydian: E - F# - G# - A - B - C# - D - E
The ♭VII chord (D major) is diatonic to E Mixolydian, containing D - F# - A
Borrowing ♭VII imports the minor 7th scale degree (D natural instead of D#)
Without the leading tone (D#), there is no pull toward dominant resolution
Mixolydian borrowing gives the progression its floating, non-resolving quality

sections.title: Double Modal Interchange
items: This progression uniquely combines borrowing from two different modes simultaneously
The ♭III comes from the parallel Aeolian (natural minor) mode
The ♭VII comes from the parallel Mixolydian mode
Only the I and IV chords are diatonic to the home major key
This 50/50 split between diatonic and borrowed chords gives the progression its distinctive power

sections.title: Soloing Scale Strategy
items: E minor pentatonic (E-G-A-B-D) works over the entire progression as a safe starting point
Use E Mixolydian (E-F#-G#-A-B-C#-D) to highlight the major tonic and ♭VII
Switch to E Dorian (E-F#-G-A-B-C#-D) over the ♭III for a smoother blend
Target the 3rd of each chord on strong beats to outline the harmony while soloing
